cards.b: A process producing genetically identical offspring from one parent. Examples: bacterial division, potato tubers, strawberry runners.
Fusion of the nuclei of two gametes to form a zygote; offspring are genetically different from each other.
A group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring.
Gamete nuclei are haploid (one set of chromosomes); the zygote nucleus is diploid (two sets).

cards.f: Functions of anther, stigma, ovary and ovule
cards.b: Anther: makes pollen. Stigma: receives pollen. Ovary: contains the ovules. Ovule: contains the female gamete.

cards.f: Define pollination and fertilisation in plants
cards.b: Pollination: transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma. Fertilisation: a pollen nucleus fuses with a nucleus in an ovule.
Large, brightly coloured, scented petals; nectar; anthers and stigma inside the flower; sticky or spiky pollen.
Small dull petals; no nectar or scent; anthers hang outside; large feathery stigmas outside; large amounts of light pollen.

cards.f: Three conditions needed for seed germination
cards.b: Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Light is not needed.

cards.f: Functions of testes, scrotum, prostate gland, urethra
cards.b: Testes: make sperm and testosterone. Scrotum: holds testes where it is cooler. Prostate: adds fluid. Urethra: carries semen/urine out.

cards.f: Functions of ovary, oviduct, uterus, cervix
cards.b: Ovary: makes eggs and oestrogen. Oviduct: carries egg; fertilisation site. Uterus: embryo develops. Cervix: muscle ring at base of uterus.
Flagellum to swim; many mitochondria for energy; enzymes in the acrosome digest the egg's jelly coat.
Large cytoplasm with energy stores; jelly coat changes at fertilisation to stop more than one sperm entering.

cards.f: Role of testosterone and oestrogen at puberty
cards.b: Control secondary sexual characteristics: testosterone (testes) in males; oestrogen (ovaries) in females.

cards.f: What is an STI, and how is HIV spread?
cards.b: STI: infection passed on by sexual contact. HIV spreads by sexual contact, blood (shared needles) and mother to baby; it may lead to AIDS.

short.q: Compare the structure of an insect-pollinated flower with a wind-pollinated flower. [3]
short.model: Insect-pollinated flowers have large, coloured, scented petals and nectar with anthers inside; wind-pollinated flowers have small petals, anthers hanging outside and large feathery stigmas.
points: stigma sticky inside versus large feathery outside

short.q: Explain why oxygen is needed for seed germination. [2]
short.model: Oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration, which releases energy for growth of the seedling.

short.q: State one advantage and one disadvantage of sexual reproduction in a wild population. [2]
short.model: Advantage: genetic variation, so some survive environmental change or disease. Disadvantage: needs two parents and is slower.

short.q: Describe what happens to the uterus lining and ovary during one menstrual cycle. [3]
short.model: The lining breaks down in menstruation, then thickens again; an egg is released from the ovary at about day 14 and the lining stays thick, breaking down if the egg is not fertilised.

short.q: State three ways in which the spread of STIs can be controlled. [3]
short.model: Use condoms, limit the number of sexual partners, and test and treat infected people.
points: testing and treating / screening blood / no shared needles
